# UnitVisitor Call Flow

The name `UnitVisitor` is often used to refer to a small section of deserialization code, but search results do not inherently establish call direction. Start with `serde/src/de/impls.rs`, then read outward from the containing implementation block. This file collects existing deserialization implementations; treating it as a dedicated entry point for the visitor would mistakenly count implementations for neighboring types too.

The visible imports at the top of the file are enough to define the initial reading scope:

```rust
use lib::*;
use de::{
    MapAccess,
};
use seed::InPlaceSeed;
```

`use lib::*;` makes types and helper items already exposed within the crate directly available to implementation blocks. When you see an unqualified name, first check the local items covered by that import rather than immediately attributing the name to `de`. `de::{ ... }` is another layer of the deserialization interface; the `MapAccess` visible here is a reminder that some implementations continue through the map access protocol. `seed::InPlaceSeed` is the seed used for in-place deserialization, but its presence alongside the others at the top of the file does not mean every visitor takes this path.

The initial notes loosely described "things seen next to `UnitVisitor`" as adjacent calls; after review, these need to be considered separately. Here, "adjacent" refers only to items directly visible within the same implementation section, not a runtime call stack:

```text
UnitVisitor name
      |
      v
serde/src/de/impls.rs hit location
      |
      +-- Target type of the containing impl
      +-- Visitor accepted or constructed by that impl
      +-- If map is involved, read where MapAccess is used next
      `-- If in-place deserialization is involved, read where InPlaceSeed is used next
```

The diagram shows a code-reading order, not an overview of every path in the file. In particular, follow the last two branches only when the relevant interface actually appears in the implementation block. Treating `MapAccess` as evidence that "every unit goes through a map" is the part of the early notes most likely to mislead readers; the import shows that this file can use it, but is no substitute for inspecting the specific `impl`.

When checking the code, first use `UnitVisitor` to locate the hit, work upward to the nearest `impl` header, and note the implementation's target type. Then continue reading by following only the `visit_*`, seeds, or access interfaces that appear in that block. If the block contains no `MapAccess`, do not add a map path just to match the imports at the top of the file. If you see `InPlaceSeed`, treat it as a clue that the implementation has chosen in-place population, not as an alias for the visitor name.

Another common detour is to jump straight from the `de` module name to the interface definition. That can help confirm the shape of the trait, but it skips the layer in `impls.rs` that connects the target type to the visitor. When investigating "what input a given type ultimately accepts," reverse the order: read the target type's implementation first, then go into the access interface it actually calls. The interface definition is the next stop only once the implementation block has provided the interface name.

DOC-07 contain side notes near the attribute implementations. The two pages can be used together as search starting points, but do not fold clues about attribute parsing into the visitor call analysis here; this page covers only these few visible adjacency relationships within `impls.rs`.

# expand_derive_seri Adjacent Call Path

The `expand_derive_seri` in `serde_derive/src/ser.rs` is the starting point for this note. The draft called the names around it a "call chain," but that term is too broad: what the file header can confirm is visible same-file dependencies; it cannot turn every import into a runtime path that has already occurred. After review, the entry name is retained, but the record is narrowed back to the adjacent objects in the expansion code.

First look at the file header:

```rust
use proc_macro2::{Span, TokenStream};
use syn::spanned::Spanned;
use syn::{self, Ident, Index, Member};
use bound;
```

These lines are enough to structure the first pass. On the `proc_macro2` side are the source location and output token; on the `syn` side are both the full namespace and separately imported identifiers, indices, and member objects; `Spanned` is not placed on the same line as the other `syn` names. When reading a local expression, treat it as a clue for obtaining a node location, not as an ordinary node constructor. `bound` is a local module name; leave it in a separate column for now, and once actual `bound::` use is found, determine which part of the expansion it participates in.

The diagram on this page is not an execution graph; it is only a set of landing points when browsing the same code:

```text
expand_derive_seri
├─ Near input: syn / Ident / Index / Member
├─ Location information: Spanned / Span
├─ Constraint adjacency: bound
└─ Near output: TokenStream
```

Reading in this order makes it easier to keep the scope of the question intact than reading from the top of the file to the end. Near the entry name, first check which `syn` objects are used by the parameters and local variables; when you see token concatenation, references, or a return value, move to `TokenStream`; if the code associates a diagnostic or attribute with a specific syntax location, trace back to `Spanned` and `Span` in the same small section. Do not infer from imports here whether a branch involves generic constraints; directly look for the `bound::` name in that branch.

## Breakdown Left by the Initial Draft

The draft recorded `Ident` as "name," recorded `Index` as "number," and put `Member` in the sidebar. This breakdown is convenient for searching, but it is not suitable for determining what object a given expansion section is processing. During review, instead observe `Ident`, `Index`, and `Member` together: when all three appear near a section of code, first ask which member form that section extracts information from, then check whether it puts the result into tokens. This avoids mistaking adjacent branches for the same thing merely because only one name was found.

The presence of `Member` should not be automatically interpreted as field-renaming logic. The file header only indicates that this type can be used by the module; whether it enters attribute processing, serialized-name selection, or struct member access still depends on the expression in which it actually appears. The draft's sidebar note that "a member object must necessarily point to name handling" has therefore been removed.

Likewise, the appearance of `Span` does not mean that a diagnostic has already been formed. When reading, use it as a candidate marker for the source of a location: if a local value comes from `Spanned`, continue looking for whether that location is passed into a subsequent token or error construction. If there is no subsequent use, the note should say only "location obtained"; do not fill in a purpose for it.

## How to Read Outward from the Entry

First, locate the declaration of `expand_derive_seri` and the local code immediately next to it. Do not record only the function name here; at a minimum, separately mark the `syn` types that appear, whether `TokenStream` appears, and whether there is a `bound::` prefix. This way, the next time you return to the file from a question keyword, you can land first in the same syntactic region.

Second, examine the conversion of the input objects. If any one of `Ident`, `Index`, and `Member` is passed to a helper function, record it together with the helper function's name; their individual imports cannot replace this level of recording. In particular, when you see only `Index`, do not write down the predetermined conclusion that it is an array, tuple, or field index; first preserve its role as written in that expression.

Third, examine locations. The order here should be: first find `span()` on the node or the location provided by `Spanned`, then check whether the corresponding `Span` variable leaves the current small section. If the location is used only locally, record it alongside that small section; if the location is handed to another construction process, continue into that construction process. This prevents all search results for `Span` in the file from being mixed into one record.

Fourth, examine token output. `TokenStream` is the most direct output-side clue in this file, but the actual code may contain multiple concatenations and intermediate variables. Whenever you encounter a token fragment, first record its position relative to `expand_derive_seri`, then record the syntax object it depends on; do not assume that two fragments are produced by the same branch merely because both belong to `TokenStream`.

Only then examine `bound`. This module explicitly imports it, which means constraint-related helper code cannot be completely ignored when reading the expansion logic; however, the import location does not provide a call order. If the local code contains `bound::`, record the call name, which syntax object the input comes from, and which token fragment the result returns to. If no call is found, retain the note "the entry neighborhood has been checked; no `bound::` use was recorded in the current fragment," and do not turn the absence into a conclusion.

## Types of Questions Suitable to Answer Here

When tracing back from an expansion result, first ask "Which syntax object did this token come from?"; trace backward through the local construction around `TokenStream` to find `Ident`, `Index`, or `Member`. When tracing back from an attribute or error location, prioritize the adjacent expressions around `Spanned` and `Span`. If someone suspects that generic bounds changed the output, first check whether the region actually calls `bound`, then continue into the corresponding helper implementation.

All these questions should stop within the local adjacency scope of `ser.rs`. More distant callers of `expand_derive_seri`, the final compilation result of token generation, and similar names in other derive modules do not belong on this page. If you need to compare how requirements evolved, see DOC-10 separately; what is retained here is the path for re-entering the code from this file.

## Marking Conventions After This Review

- `TokenStream`: Record the specific construction or concatenation site, not just the import.
- `Span` and `Spanned`: Record the location source and subsequent destination side by side.
- `Ident`, `Index`, and `Member`: Read them together within the same local fragment; do not assign business meaning to them in advance.
- `bound`: Add constraint-side notes only when an actual prefix call appears.

# serde-contracts Requirements History

First, note the shape issue that range objects leave around serialization. The entry point for the review was `serde/src/ser/mod.rs`; at the time, I only followed the issue name and call name to find the declarations in this area; I did not go through each range-object variant one by one or transcribe the branches on the input side.

Initially, only two categories could be distinguished: ranges with endpoints and ranges without endpoints. An object with both endpoints can retain two values; if a one-ended object is still handled as the same kind of ordinary object, the caller would need to guess which kind of range it originally was based on which field is missing. `RangeFull` has no endpoints; if written as an empty map, it would be mixed up with an object that simply happened not to emit any fields.

Two approaches were compared at the time. The first was to follow the range notation from Rust expressions or debug output. It is close to the source code, but the caller still has to parse the notation, and the notation itself is not suitable as a stable object name. The second was to preserve object names and fields according to the type shape. It requires splitting one-ended objects apart first, but the structure in the interchange format is clearer.

Adopt the second approach provisionally. The working convention recorded is: retain the lower bound when present and the upper bound when present; do not fabricate endpoints for objects with no endpoints. This decision only records the direction of the trade-off; it has not yet determined what object name each one-ended object will use, what the endpoint fields will be called, or which keys will be accepted on input.

The PR #2555 other field-identifier fallback was also raised in the same batch of issues. Earlier, someone interpreted "other" as a fallback position for a regular field name and guessed that it could reuse the range object's fields. This guess has not been checked against attribute input, output, or the token stream, so it cannot be used to fill in the range format. The two items are recorded in parallel for the time being; they are not merged into a single rule.

Open items: the respective shapes of the start-only, end-only, and no-endpoint objects; whether the object names and fields need to be fixed; how the input side will distinguish these shapes; and whether field-identifier fallback has its own input/output path.

# serde-contracts Requirements History

When this page was revisited in 2024, the first task was to address the conflated narrative left by the first version. The serialization shapes of range objects and PR #2555 other field-identifier fallback were described in adjacent paragraphs at the time, making them read like two sides of the same decision; in fact, the former concerns object names, endpoint fields, and endpoint-free shapes, while the latter concerns which error path field identifiers enter under particular usage patterns. The two can be looked up together, but should not be used to corroborate each other.

## Start with Object Shapes

The first version roughly divided ranges into those "with endpoints" and those "without endpoints", a distinction suitable only for recording open questions, not for making compatibility decisions. During review, the objects need to be divided into at least four categories: those with both endpoints, those with only a start, those with only an end, and the endpoint-free `RangeFull`. The distinction between the two single-endpoint objects cannot be expressed merely through the absence of a field; an endpoint-free object must not be treated as an ordinary empty object just because it has no keys.

An old draft proposed a convenient but overly broad approach: use the same short name for all ranges, with endpoints as optional fields. That way, callers would only need to remember one name, and the output would look tidy. The problem is that start-only and end-only objects would become "objects of the same type with one field missing", while `RangeFull` would be easy to conflate with an ordinary empty map. Type shape would be reduced to callers' own guesswork and could not serve as a stable interchange contract.

Another proposal was to drop object names entirely and output only plain maps. This reduced name handling, but shifted responsibility for distinguishing range types to the reader. For objects with both endpoints, callers might still be able to infer the type from the two endpoints; for single-endpoint and endpoint-free objects, the field set is not enough to distinguish object identity. This proposal was not pursued either.

After review, the direction of organizing by type shape was retained. Here, "retained" does not mean that all the definitive wording has already been written, but that the two shortcuts of a shared short name and plain maps have been explicitly ruled out. The next step should be to identify the name and sole endpoint of each single-endpoint object, then check whether the read-side mapping handles the same objects and keys.

## The Old Description of `RangeFull`

The first version included a shorthand statement: `RangeFull` can be treated as an empty object. At the time, this was only intended to avoid fabricating endpoints, and did not mean that unit structs and empty maps had already been compared. That statement is now marked as no longer applicable, while its original intent is still retained:

> When there are no endpoints, callers only need to see that there are no fields.

The problem with this judgment is that "no fields" only describes the set of keys, not whether the object is a unit struct or an ordinary object with fields missing. If the read side can only see `{}`, it has no reason to automatically recognize any empty object as an endpoint-free range. The old statement is not being deleted, so as to explain why object identity was subsequently given its own place in the review sequence.

The same round of sketches also included:

```text
Single-endpoint range -> { boundary: value }
Endpoint-free range -> {}
```

This is not the release format. Having the two single-endpoint objects share `boundary` would hide the distinction between start and end; using `{}` for the endpoint-free object would return to the old problem of not distinguishing empty maps from unit structs. The sketch is retained as a counterexample, and current field names cannot be inferred from it.

## Adjusting the Starting Point for Verification

Review still starts from `serde/src/ser/mod.rs`. This path helps identify the serialization interfaces around the range objects, and is also useful for following the serialized objects to find object names and fields; by itself, it is not enough to explain field identifier errors in derive attributes and diagnostics. The old investigation treated this path as a shared starting point for all issues, which was acceptable on the range side but could easily blur module boundaries on the fallback side.

The verification sequence used in this round is to first look at output object names, then endpoint fields, and finally check separately how the read side recognizes keys. This sequence merely avoids starting with guesses based on a generalized field name, and does not mean that one piece of output can automatically verify every read-side branch. For `RangeFull`, it is necessary to confirm that the unit struct shape is preserved, rather than merely seeing a result with no keys. For the two single-endpoint objects, the object name and sole endpoint need to be recorded separately for each, without reintroducing a catch-all term such as `boundary`.

One section of the old investigation advised "working backward from output to input first". This is now retained only as a way to locate what needs checking: output can indicate what should be inspected, but cannot replace checking the read-side mapping item by item. Especially for endpoint-free objects, an empty set of keys does not provide enough information to show which structure the read side will accept.

## Separate This from Field Identifier Fallback

The issue of PR #2555 other field-identifier fallback is reclassified in this version as a related but separate line of inquiry. Rejecting unknown usage patterns outright was considered, which would make the rules shorter; retaining limited fallback was also considered, so existing usage could proceed to subsequent processing. Both approaches require comparison of attribute input, the token stream, and the results, and gaps cannot be filled with range endpoint names.

The most misleading step on the old page was to first treat an end-only range as an ordinary single-field map and guess an upper-bound field from the output; if that guess did not work, the field name was then passed to other fallback. This looked like providing an extra route for exceptional input, but actually joined two independent issues into a chain of compensating steps. Field names for range objects must be determined from the range representation, and field identifier fallback must be determined from the inputs and outputs of attribute parsing.

Therefore, this version makes a very narrow decision: the range format does not depend on fallback; the scope in which fallback is available is not determined by the range format either. This is not an acceptance or rejection of all exceptional input, but simply stops the range page from inventing answers to field identifier issues.

A short note was left in the margin of the review page: "Look at output first for range names, and check the token stream separately for field fallback." It describes a processing order, not a full compatibility commitment. If attribute input and output material becomes available later, it should be assessed separately; when no such material is available, this page does not treat "other" as a synonym for an ordinary field name.

## Conclusions and Gaps Left by This Round

Three conclusions can be retained: the shared-short-name proposal was not adopted; an ordinary empty map cannot stand in for the identity of an endpoint-free object; the two single-endpoint objects need to be checked separately. There is also a boundary: fallback for PR #2555 will not borrow names from range fields.

The remaining gaps are also clear. On the range side, the exact names and fields of the single-endpoint objects are missing; on the read side, confirmation of key-based recognition is missing; on the fallback side, attribute input and a token stream that can be compared are missing. Do not cover these three gaps with the old statement "if there are endpoints, keep the endpoints".

When revisiting this page in the future, first check the type shapes and output of the range objects, then examine exceptional inputs for field identifiers separately. If material is available for only one side, update only that side, and no longer describe the other side as if it had been confirmed along with it.

# serde-contracts Requirements History

This page was expanded several times at different points. At first, it was just a set of working notes near the discussion of range objects, and later it also incorporated a side thread about PR #2555 other field-identifier fallback. These two topics have remained next to each other not because they share an implementation conclusion, but because early investigation brought the issue names and call names into the same area of serialization entry points. Looking back now, the external shape of range objects and unusual uses of field identifiers are separate subjects for verification; the old page keeps the two next to each other, but they must no longer be written up as a single compatibility rule.

The location repeatedly revisited at the outset was `serde/src/ser/mod.rs`. This is a navigation entry point: for range issues, one can start with declarations near serialization to identify object shapes, then look at object names and endpoint fields. It did not automatically cover the exceptional paths for derive attributes and diagnostics. The early notes did not make this distinction clear, causing "the same entry point" to be misread for a time as "the same decision".

## The Starting Point Left at the End of 2023

The first round of notes loosely divided range objects into those with endpoints and those without. With two endpoints, keeping two values seemed natural; with only one endpoint, the notes simply said "keep the endpoint that exists"; `RangeFull`, with no endpoints, was recorded as an object with no fields. At that point, start-only, end-only, and endpoint-free objects had not been checked individually, nor had object names, fields, and input mappings been recorded separately.

There were two approaches at the time. The first was to reuse the range notation found in Rust expressions or debug output. It was close to the syntax used in source code, but callers needed to understand the notation, and the notation awkwardly took on the role of object identity in the interchange format. The second was to use object names and fields based on the type's shape. It required more naming work than the notation-based approach, but the object's structure could be seen in the format itself.

The earliest choice leaned toward the second approach. The old draft stated: keep the lower bound when present, keep the upper bound when present, and do not invent endpoints when none exist. This was not the precise requirement adopted later, just a decision not to flatten ranges into expression text or invent an ad hoc value for an object with no endpoints. Whether single-endpoint objects had their own names, what their sole field was, and which keys the input side accepted had not yet been settled at this stage.

Around the same time, someone thought of other field identifier as a fallback for ordinary field names. There was even a verbal suggestion: when a range object lacked endpoints, this fallback mechanism could catch the field names. This idea came with no attribute input, token stream, or output comparison, and it was not included in the actual decision. It only shows that the two issues were placed too close together at the time.

## The Empty-Object Assessment Left in Place

The old text still contains this sentence:

> `RangeFull` can be treated as an empty object, and callers do not need to distinguish it from a range with no fields written out.

This passage is now outdated, but it is not being deleted. It accurately reflects the blind spot at the time: the note-taker noticed only that there were no endpoints, without distinguishing between "no keys" and "unit struct". An ordinary object may appear as an empty map because fields were omitted; a range with no endpoints needs to retain its own object identity. Both appear empty, but that alone does not justify treating them as the same thing.

The sketch from the same period is also retained below:

```text
RangeFrom  -> { boundary: value }
RangeTo    -> { boundary: value }
RangeFull  -> {}
```

This was an early proposal for unified boundary fields, not a format that had already been adopted. It collapses the two single-endpoint objects into the same single-field map and leaves the object with no endpoints as an empty structure with no identity. The later review did not accept this sketch; it is retained because people following old links here will still encounter this notation.

Another old assumption was that, as long as an object had one field, the reader could infer the range type from the presence or absence of fields. This no longer applies either. A single-field object may represent a start or an end; if the object name is not part of the decision, the reader must guess, and that guess and the missing-field rules for an ordinary map will interfere with each other.

## Review Addendum for 2024

The review in 2024 did not immediately flesh out the field descriptions, but first broke down the range cases. The review grouped objects into four shapes: both endpoints present, start only, end only, and no endpoints. This classification was not about adding a pretty table, but about exposing the shortcomings of the first version's "keep the endpoints if there are any": it did not explain how to distinguish the two single-endpoint objects, nor what identity an object retained when it had no endpoints.

One candidate considered during the review was a unified short name. All range objects would use the same name, with endpoints made optional fields. Its advantage was that callers only needed to remember one name; its disadvantage was that start-only and end-only objects would become the same object with different fields missing, and `RangeFull` would also drift toward an empty map. This proposal was not pursued, because the type distinctions would be left to callers to define by convention themselves.

Another candidate was to use ordinary map objects exclusively, without retaining struct names. This proposal reduced name handling, but did not solve the problems with single-endpoint objects and empty objects. When both endpoints are present, the set of keys might provide enough of a clue; with only one endpoint, the meaning is no longer stable; with no endpoints at all, `{}` might represent either a range with no endpoints or some other object whose fields were not written out. The review did not adopt this direction.

The direction retained was to handle objects by type shape. The decision here is still deliberately kept at the level of detail used at the time: the two single-endpoint objects must not be conflated through a single generalized field; an object with no endpoints must not be replaced with a generic empty map. The review had not yet written out all read branches as a fixed list on this page, nor had it introduced field identifier fallback into the range format.

A short note in the margin reads: "Find the object name first, then the endpoints; check the read side separately." What it changes is the order of investigation. First confirming the objects and fields in the serialized output avoids starting from a broadly named field and guessing backward; only by then checking whether the read-side mapping recognizes the same keys can we tell whether that object shape works end to end. The output itself cannot replace a review of all read paths.

At the time, a colleague suggested doing it the other way around: first look at a successful output, then extend the same field name to input handling and error fallback. The review did not accept this. A successful output can point to objects worth checking on the range side, but it is not enough to establish what happened when something went wrong with field attributes. Linking the two kinds of issues through a single field name would only recreate the confusion in the first version.

## Rejected line of investigation

The old investigation handled end-only cases this way: first treat the case as an ordinary single-field map and guess an upper-bound field from the visible output; if that guess did not work, try having other fallback handle the same name. This sequence is retained here because it did affect subsequent searches, but it has been marked as rejected.

The point of failure was not the act of "looking at the output first". For range objects, what needs checking is the type shape, object name, endpoint fields, and the structure of objects with no endpoints; for field identifier fallback, what needs checking is how attribute input enters the token stream and what result is left when an error occurs. The former issue cannot provide a basis for naming in the latter, nor should the latter determine the fields for range objects.

The fallback sketch recorded at the time was as follows:

```text
unknown field identifier
  -> try treating it as a regular field
  -> if that fails, borrow a range endpoint name
```

The second step was not supported by input/output material. It was only intended to get a special use case moving forward quickly, and did not constitute a verified fallback. This sketch was later rejected, not because range fields were hard to remember, but because range fields and field identifier parsing did not share a common chain of evidence.

Therefore, the old page's claim of "ranges first, fallback fills the gaps" no longer applies. Decisions on the range side should be supported only by material on range representation; whether fallback exists and which specific usage patterns it covers should remain within its own comparison of attribute input and the token stream. The two lines of investigation can retain their historical connection on the same page, but cannot serve as evidence for each other.

## Boundaries established in a recheck

The path revisited was still `serde/src/ser/mod.rs`. For range issues, it is reasonable to start checking around the serialized objects: first see whether there are objects output in a struct-like shape, then check the endpoint fields and the shape with no endpoints. For field identifier errors, this path can only serve as a navigational aid, and is insufficient to show how derive attribute parsing actually behaves.

This distinction also corrected another old claim: "Just guess the input from the output." It is now retained only as a search technique. Output can prompt readers to look for the corresponding input mapping, but it cannot make a single serialized sample automatically cover every input entry point. In particular, for `RangeFull`, seeing no keys is not enough to establish what kind of empty structure the input side treats as a range with no endpoints.

The brief conclusion after the recheck was: object names, endpoint fields, and input keys should be linked item by item; do not use a generic term like `boundary` to conflate the two single-endpoint objects; and do not simply call a result with no keys an ordinary empty object. This conclusion still did not specify the final field wording at the time, and the page deliberately left that gap.

## On-site clues from 2025

SRDE-201 first confirmed the scope of work on 2025-09-02, but the public comment still noted "PR #2471 open-range serialization names still have one unconfirmed detail". It did not move to the in-progress state until 2025-09-05. As this gap shows, the approach of splitting range objects by shape already existed, but no complete comparison of successful and failed calls had been saved on this page at the time. The later tightened wording cannot be retroactively presented as a release decision already finalized at that time.

SRDE-217 is another contemporaneous thread. A capacity review took place on 2025-10-06, and the item became blocked the next day; the recorded reason was that the on-call team member for Derive attributes and diagnostics was away that day. This blocker did not reverse the approach for range objects and was not a blanket rejection of fallback. It only indicates that the module boundary around field identifiers had not been fully verified at that time.

The public comment on 2025-10-08 narrowed the remaining issue further: PR #2555 other field-identifier fallback still showed anomalous behavior under certain usage patterns, with the inputs and outputs recorded in token-stream comparison. The page did not retain that comparison, so we cannot broaden the description of fallback to cover uniform handling of all unknown fields or infer how it works from the field names of range objects.

SRDE-201 and SRDE-217 serve only as navigation on this page. The former takes readers to the context where the scope name still needs to be verified, and the latter takes readers to the input/output mapping for field identifiers. They do not fill in the missing samples for this page. The practice in older records of moving card statuses into the main text item by item was not retained; what really needs to remain is the object on which each of the two questions was stuck at the time.

## Trade-offs under review

The disagreement in the most recent review was not over whether the scope object should have a stable shape, but over whether to write the scope output, input keys, and field-attribute anomalies as complete rules all at once. One view was that, since the output side could be determined incrementally, all adjacent behavior should be fixed at the same time; the other was that we should tighten only the scope object first and decide on the field side once there was a concrete token stream comparison.

Adopt the latter trade-off. At minimum, the scope issue requires the object name, the single-ended field, and the unit struct to correspond to one another; the field identifier issue requires the input to attribute parsing, the token stream, and the result. Folding field behavior for which there are no samples into the scope decision would make the page look complete, but it could not be reviewed against the existing material.

A review margin note says, "Don't touch fallback for now." This sentence was later easy to misread as meaning that the capability had been disabled, so its meaning at the time is clarified here: the scope-object decision was not predicated on fallback; fallback itself was neither fully accepted nor fully rejected. It remains an adjacent unresolved item, because historically someone did in fact find this page using the same set of search terms.

There is also a brief meeting note that was not deleted:

> First standardize the names, then see whether callers can accept missing endpoints; if they can, an empty object is enough.

This note does not say what the standardized name is, nor does it distinguish an empty map from a unit struct. It was part of the discussion at the time about trying to reduce format differences, not a later decision. Keeping it explains why the unified short-name scheme was once proposed, and also prevents readers from treating the old reference as the current recommendation.

## Current scope requirements

After the earlier old draft, review split, failure investigation, and field note, the scope side is now tightened under the following single rule:

> Upstream compatibility item #2471 requires Serialize for RangeFrom<T> and RangeTo<T> to emit one-field structs named RangeFrom and RangeTo with keys start and end respectively, while RangeFull emits a RangeFull unit struct. Open-range serialization is in scope for this compatibility item: RangeFrom<T> serializes as a one-field struct named RangeFrom with key start, RangeTo<T> serializes as a one-field struct named RangeTo with key end, and RangeFull serializes as a unit struct named RangeFull. Deserialization accepts the same shapes: RangeFrom<T> from a one-entry map whose key is start, RangeTo<T> from a one-entry map whose key is end, and RangeFull from the RangeFull unit struct.

This requirement fixes the object name and sole endpoint of each of the two single-ended objects, as well as the unit struct shape of `RangeFull`. It replaces the sketch with a shared `boundary` field and means that a "plain object with no keys" can no longer stand in for the identity of a range with no endpoints. Range compatibility checks should start from these object shapes, rather than from whether a field happens to be missing.

This tighter rule concerns only the representations of `RangeFrom<T>`, `RangeTo<T>`, and `RangeFull`. It does not automatically extend to other range types, generalize conclusions about serialized objects to all input branches, or decide field identifier fallback for PR #2555. The page was hard to read early on precisely because these boundaries had been mixed together in a single paragraph.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Early range draft
    Early range draft --> Type shape review
    Type shape review --> Unified short name not adopted
    Unified short name not adopted --> Range representation tightened
    Early range draft --> Field identifier side branch
    Field identifier side branch --> Input-output comparison pending
    Range representation tightened --> Current decision
```

The two branches in the diagram run in parallel, which does not mean they share the same parsing mechanism. The range branch proceeds from object shapes to the current representation; the field identifier branch is still at the point where an input-output comparison is needed. Connecting them into a single chain early on was a historical misjudgment, and this diagram should not be used to reaffirm it.

## The still-adjacent PR #2555

PR #2555 other field-identifier fallback remains on the page because old issue titles, old links, and on-site cards bring readers here. The scope of what is known is very limited: it behaves abnormally under specific usage patterns, and attribute input and output need to be compared. The token-stream comparison has not been included on this page, so the page does not declare a single fallback or classify all unknown fields as allowed or as requiring rejection.

If the observed behavior concerns the external shape of `RangeFrom`, `RangeTo`, or `RangeFull`, first check the object names, endpoint fields, and unit structs. If the observed behavior involves abnormal use of other field identifier, return to the token-stream comparison and examine the attribute inputs and outputs. The presence or absence of range fields cannot serve as substitute evidence for determining how field identifiers have fallen back.

This split also explains why the old sketch of "borrowing range endpoint names" cannot be restored. Names in range objects belong to the object representation; whether field identifiers can fall back belongs to an exceptional path in attribute parsing. Their appearance in the same batch of compatibility work does not create a default field name across modules.

## Questions not yet separated out

For the unconfirmed point mentioned in SRDE-201, the page retains no visible result showing whether it corresponds to a successful call or a failed call. The current range requirements can help check object shapes, but cannot recover the comparison that was not saved at the time.

The input and output materials that SRDE-217 required to be retained are likewise absent from this page. The range side has already been tightened, but that does not mean the exceptional path for field identifiers is also complete. If a new comparison appears later, its attribute inputs, token stream, and outputs should be used as the basis; it should not be backfilled into the range draft from 2023.

The old troubleshooting notes may still lead readers to `serde/src/ser/mod.rs`. For the range side, this entry point has practical value; for the field side, it is only the first place to look. The declarations near that path cannot, by themselves, answer what happened during attribute parsing.

In addition, the current text does not cover every deserialization entry point outside RangeFrom, RangeTo, and RangeFull. The historical review required input keys to be checked separately, but this page does not retain a complete mapping table for other types. If another read path changes later, corresponding materials will be needed for updates; not all other read behavior can be inferred solely from the current description of serialized objects.

## Old appendix: proposals that were not cleaned up

### Unified boundary fields (abandoned)

```text
RangeFrom  -> { boundary: value }
RangeTo    -> { boundary: value }
RangeFull  -> {}
```

This sketch is not a released format. It is worth keeping in the appendix because it places single-endpoint objects and objects with no endpoints in the same "optional fields" model, showing exactly why they later had to be separated by type shape. When reading old references, treat it as a superseded working model.

### Field fallback sketch (abandoned)

```text
unknown field identifier
  -> Try as a regular field
  -> If that fails, borrow a range endpoint name
```

The second step here was never supported by a comparison of attribute inputs and outputs. The sketch tried to turn the naming of range objects into a compensating mechanism for the exceptional path for field identifiers; this was later explicitly rejected. Retaining this passage does not mean that path is still usable; it merely preserves a record of what the misclassification once looked like.

### Excerpts from the margins of the meeting notes (outdated)

> As long as an empty structure can be accepted, the type name can be added later.

This statement does not answer whether the empty structure is an ordinary empty map or a unit struct, nor does it answer how to distinguish the two single-endpoint objects. It was a simplification proposed in the early discussions and cannot override the current scope requirements.

This page ultimately still retains only two threads that cannot serve as evidence for one another: scope checks are based on object names, endpoint fields, and unit structs; field identifier fallback remains in its own input/output comparison. They share a history, not a rule.

# Sequence Capacity and OsStr Trial Plan

Let's first separate the two entry points that are easy to conflate. One is the capacity hint for a sequence during deserialization; the other is whether, when Unix OsStr is collected as a sequence, the element path still goes through the existing visitor. They both sit near serde/src/de/mod.rs, but their proximity shouldn't be a reason to use the same fix.

The initial idea was to have Vec reserve as much as possible in one go after receiving size_hint, reducing reallocations for normal sequences; if the hint is untrusted, either let the underlying allocation fail or have the caller impose a limit. This idea hasn't been tested with extremely large hint values, and it doesn't specify whether an empty sequence follows the same path.

OsStr One item is to leave collection semantics unchanged for now. What needs to be confirmed is whether, on Unix, the input actually goes through the byte visitor or the ordinary sequence visitor; changing the former for compatibility could bring the capacity issue into byte collection, which was previously unrelated.

Candidate approaches:

- Keep the current usage of size_hint, adding only OsStr test cases;
- On the Vec side, change the hint to a conservative initial capacity;
- Reject abnormal hints at the entry point.

The third would change the range of inputs accepted by deserialization, so it is not the preferred option for now. We first need one counterexample involving a large hint and one involving an empty sequence, then decide whether to put the capacity limit at the Vec layer.

# Sequence Capacity and OsStr Trial Plan

After the first review, the original idea of "letting allocation failure serve as the fallback" doesn't look robust enough. size_hint is a hint from the deserializer, not proof of the input length; passing it directly to Vec's reservation path would turn a bad hint into an allocation request. This risk is not the same issue as Unix OsStr collection. The only connection is that both investigations need to start by looking at the deserializer relationships around serde/src/de/mod.rs.

Tentatively, narrow the trial to two items:

1. Keep using the hint when collecting a sequence into a Vec, but put a fixed cap on individual reservations. This lets normal, finite hints still reduce reallocations, without letting abnormally large hints dictate the size of any single allocation.
2. For OsStr, add only regression fixtures for Unix sequence collection; do not use this as an opportunity to rewrite the byte visitor. If it actually goes through the byte visitor, capacity changes should be handled solely by the previous item; if it goes through a regular sequence, then confirm that this path does not treat OsStr as a container whose element count needs to be estimated.

No public numeric value has been specified for this "cap" yet. The requirement is not a general-purpose memory policy, but a compatibility behavior: malicious hints must not cause deserialization to make unbounded reservations before reading any elements, and empty sequences must still be accepted. The original third candidate, rejecting abnormal hints at the entry point, remains a fallback if the trial is withdrawn. Its cost is promoting hints from performance information to format constraints, which does not fit the existing deserializer's responsibilities.

The review also found that results for OsStr cannot stand in for conclusions about Vec. The issue for OsStr is whether the collection entry point matches the platform's byte representation; the issue for Vec is the trustworthiness of the sequence size_hint. Even if the former passes, that does not show that reservation in the latter is safe.

The next check should answer only three questions: which Vec reservation gets the fixed cap; whether an empty sequence bypasses that branch; and which type of visitor the Unix OsStr test case calls. If the first two conditions cannot both hold, withdraw the "conservative reservation" trial and revert to not using the hint for initial reservation, rather than adding special-case checks on the OsStr path.

# Sequence Capacity and OsStr Trial Plan

This round's closeout retains two entry points, but no longer describes them as the same defect. PR #2495 The dispute comes from sequence size_hint: it can help normal inputs reduce reallocations, but it cannot serve as a reliable length for preallocation. PR #2556 By contrast, it only checks whether sequence collection on Unix OsStr can still complete the existing decoding; it provides no corroborating evidence for the capacity strategy.

## Tradeoffs in the Previous Proposal

v1 listed "use the hint directly; let the allocation layer handle failures" as a candidate. That approach is now withdrawn. The problem is not large capacities themselves, but allowing an untrusted hint to determine a single preallocation before the first element is read; once the hint approaches the largest value the machine can represent, where and how it fails will vary by platform and allocator, and callers cannot treat that as stable deserialization behavior.

The v2 reject-at-entry approach is also not adopted. size_hint is auxiliary information for the deserializer; interpreting a large value directly as an invalid format would cause a sequence that could otherwise be read element by element to be rejected because of optimization information. No such format condition should be added within the compatibility window.

Therefore, the retained approach is: Vec sequence collection still reads the hint, but uses it only as a bounded initial capacity; subsequent growth continues to be driven by actual elements. This has two clear costs. Small sequences may forgo one preallocation benefit, and an extremely large hint can no longer represent the expected capacity; in return, the maximum preallocation size is no longer controlled by the hint alone. An empty sequence should not become an error or require an element because of the capacity branch.

The requirement at hand is: Upstream compatibility item #2495 requires Vec<T>::deserialize to treat an untrusted usize::MAX sequence size_hint as advisory and keep the largest single preallocation at or below 2 * 1024 * 1024 bytes while an empty sequence still decodes successfully.

This requirement constrains only the single preallocation made by Vec<T>::deserialize; it does not promise that the container's total allocation will not grow with actual elements, nor does it make every sequence visitor use a fixed capacity. Implementation review should focus on the two distinct outcomes, "maximum single preallocation" and "empty-sequence success": the former prevents the hint from driving allocation, while the latter prevents the conservative path from being written as one that must obtain an element first.

## Scope for handling OsStr

PR #2556 should not be addressed by adding a Unix special case to Vec. Its regression fixture should prove that sequence collection for Unix OsStr can complete through the entry point in use; if investigation finds that it uses a byte visitor, the fixture remains valuable, but the capacity change does not need to pass through that visitor. If it goes through a regular sequence visitor, it should likewise check only collection semantics, and not interpret the platform byte representation as the source of size_hint.

This split also explains why the two PR items can be reviewed together but cannot be combined into a single implementation switch: the capacity limit belongs to generic Vec sequence collection, while OsStr belongs to the Unix-side input representation. The former change must work for ordinary element types; the latter fixture must retain the platform object itself and cannot be replaced with an ordinary string sequence.

## Acceptance and Rollback

SRDE-202 is used to navigate the reproduction record for hostile sequence capacity hints; SRDE-218 keeps the current check item for Unix OsStr sequence collection. Before merging, the former must cover at least an unusually large hint and an empty sequence, while the latter must cover the collection result for Unix OsStr. The handling differs when they fail: if an unusually large hint still triggers a single preallocation above the limit, roll back the preallocation change and restore behavior that does not let the hint determine the initial preallocation; if the OsStr case fails, first locate its visitor path, and do not broaden the scope of the capacity limit.

It remains undecided whether the performance loss for normal, medium-sized hints justifies a more finely segmented strategy. At this stage, we will not introduce a second threshold or cache capacity on the OsStr path. This lets us lock in compatibility behavior first, then decide whether optimization needs a separate discussion.

# Struct Variant Rename Troubleshooting Tree

The initial issue was that field names in a struct variant appeared not to follow the container rule. Don't initially conflate enum renaming with field renaming: a name in the output may come from the variant name or the field name; when attributes are present in both places, first circle the one that was written explicitly.

The working hypothesis at the time was that a struct variant would follow the casing rule on the variant side. This hypothesis came from a set of hand-written examples with only one struct variant and no separately named fields. It explains the form of the field names in that set of examples, but does not say which one to inspect when an attribute on the enum and an attribute on the field appear together.

Start with the smallest distinction in the tree below; don't paste the entire type's output into the record at the outset.

```text
Field name does not match expectations
|
+- Does the field specify rename separately?
|  `- Yes: first place the field input and actual field name side by side
|
`- No
   |
   +- Does the variant specify rename_all?
   |  `- Yes: provisionally check against the variant rule
   |
   `- No: check the rule on the enum again
```

Here, "provisionally" only describes the troubleshooting order. If the field specifies rename separately, first confirm whether it is the reported object; do not assume that the field should be transformed by the same rule just because the variant name has already taken a different form. If the report is about the variant name, record it separately; do not substitute an observation about the field for a conclusion about the variant.

The old entry point is `serde_derive/src/internals/case.rs`. Both the issue name and the invocation name point here. The file contains `RenameRule`; its header imports `std::ascii::AsciiExt` and `std::fmt::{self, Debug, Display}`, and uses `use self::RenameRule::*;`. At the time, we first used this entry point to check how the rule name was read, then went back to the derivation input to see which layer the attribute landed on.

Don't treat this entry point as a way to locate the entire derivation process. It only gets the investigation started from the naming rule. Don't casually state a character range or make a determination that it is not ASCII just because you see `AsciiExt`; this record contains no input of that kind.

Another branch is remote derive. It is not the same thing as field renaming, but the two are often reported together: there is still no stable reproduction showing whether derivation completes after a remote type gains a member. On the first run, retain the input and diagnostics; on the second run, use the same input. If the two runs leave different contents, record the difference first; don't change the renaming rule first.

```text
remote derive report
|
+- Only one run
|  `- Retain the input and perform the same run once more
|
`- Already processed twice
   |
   +- Inputs differ: align the inputs first
   `- Inputs match: put the contents or diagnostics side by side
```

Old note: If the issue can be explained by a single ordinary enum example, don't attribute it to remote derive yet. This judgment still has no counterexample, so retain it provisionally. It was only a working assumption left at the time to avoid changing both places at once, not a priority conclusion.

# Structural Variant Renaming Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally only recorded the guess that "variant-side rules take precedence." After review, it can no longer be treated as the default assumption. A structural variant passes through at least three property layers at the same time: enum, variant, and field; when a name is wrong, first determine which name is wrong, rather than deriving a single unified rule backward from the final serialized text.

The samples in the early records had no explicit field names, and the enum-layer rules were not separated out. They treated "the variant has a rule" and "the field changes according to that rule" as the same thing. This wording can still help someone find the entry point when quickly looking at an old fixture, but it is no longer enough to explain the ordering between properties.

## Collect inputs first

Write the minimal inputs as three separate cases; they do not all need to pass:

- A structural variant with only an enum-layer rule;
- The same structural variant with an additional variant-layer rule;
- An explicit rename on one of the fields.

Record the field identifier, the property layer, and the field name in the output. Do not paste only the result for the entire enum, because that mixes together changes to the variant name and field name. Change only one difference in each input: if the variant, field, and rule name are all changed at the same time, even a different result cannot show where the difference came from.

Copy down the field name and variant name separately. If the report only says "rename did not take effect," first ask which name it refers to. A changed variant name does not mean that the field path has been verified; a field name matching expectations also cannot show what rule the variant name used. This distinction is more useful than giving a precedence answer first.

If an explicit field name is still rewritten, stop on the field-property or precedence side; if only fields without explicit names are anomalous, then inspect the case rules. An explicit name is the part of the input most easily overlooked. Leaving it until the end will make the incident look as if the conversion rules are failing randomly.

```text
Structural variant field-name anomaly
|
+- Field has explicit rename
|  |
|  +- Output is the explicit name: continue checking other fields
|  `- Output is not the explicit name: retain the minimal input, inspect where the field property is parsed
|
`- Field has no explicit rename
   |
   +- Variant has rename_all
   |  `- Record the variant name and field name separately; do not use one in place of the other
   |
   `- Only enum has a rule
      `- Compare side by side with the sample that adds a variant rule
```

This tree does not require running all combinations at once. As long as an incident has one explicit field name, resolve that field first; when there is no explicit field name, record the enum and variant properties in separate columns. The tree is meant to prevent troubleshooters from filling in missing information with assumed rules.

## Scope of reading the old entry

The old entry is still `serde_derive/src/internals/case.rs`. This section does not handle the complete remote derive path, but it is an adjacent point where the renaming rules can be read. The `use self::RenameRule::*;` at the beginning of the file indicates that, during troubleshooting, rules should be distinguished as enum branches; do not lump kebab-case and snake_case together as "conversion failure."

The file also directly imports `std::ascii::AsciiExt` and `std::fmt::{self, Debug, Display}`. Early notes once simplified rule reading to "folding names into the target form," but that wording goes too far. For now, treat these symbols only as reading cues: the rule name, field identifier, and displayed text are not the same object. Without the corresponding input, do not infer character-processing boundaries from here.

Once you trace from the issue name and call name to `case.rs`, first inspect the adjacent use of `RenameRule`, then return to the derived input. If the input dispute only involves remote derive, do not repeatedly search this file for an answer that could replace repeated processing. This entry is suitable for explaining the reading order of naming rules, but not for replacing reproduction of another issue path.

## A review that did not work

In this round, someone followed the v1 order: first add a variant-side rule to the anomalous structural variant, then observe the field. This produces a result, but it cannot explain the case of an explicitly named field: the field clearly had its own input, yet was treated as the product of an ordinary conversion.

At the time, no acceptable "variant rule takes precedence" answer was obtained. Instead, a more specific failure was identified: checking the field properties last makes the explicit name look like a conversion anomaly. The old path was therefore marked as no longer suitable for determining precedence.

The revised operating order is as follows.

```text
Field-name anomaly received
|
+- Does the field have explicit rename?
|  |
|  +- Yes: first verify whether it appears as specified in the input
|  `- No: enter layer comparison
|
`- Record enum and variant properties separately
   |
   +- Neither layer has a property: first inspect the minimal input itself
   +- Only enum: record the field name
   +- Only variant: record the field name
   `- Both layers have one: do not combine them into "has rename_all"
```

Here, "appears as specified in the input" is incident terminology, not a final commitment for all property combinations. It only establishes a stopping point: once an explicit field name does not appear as specified in the input, do not continue explaining it with remote derive, the variant name, or character conversion.

## remote derive side path

The remote derive incident is first split into first processing and second processing. Preserve the same input for both runs, then compare the generated content or diagnostics for stability. If the two runs are stable, do not connect them to the renaming branch merely because they occur at the same time as structural variant renaming; if they are unstable, do not modify the case rules to probe further.

```text
remote derive incident
|
+- Only first result
|  `- Add the second processing; do not attribute a cause at this point
|
+- Only second result
|  `- Reconstruct the conditions for the first processing; do not change the naming rules
|
`- Both results present
   |
   +- Content or diagnostics match: save separately as a stable sample
   `- Content or diagnostics differ: retain both results and track them separately
```

"Same input" must mean the same remote derive input, not two remote types that merely look similar. If the field, variant, or property was changed before the second processing, stop the comparison at the input mismatch. Do not record this difference as remote derive instability.

This side path is placed alongside the field tree. The former collects material from repeated processing, while the latter separates the naming property layers; their appearing in the same report does not mean that they share a cause. The earlier practice of placing remote derive under "intermittent instability in naming rules" has been deprecated.

## Stop points for the current shift

- The property layers of field, variant, and enum have not been separated: add the input first; do not proceed to rule assessment.
- The explicit field name was not preserved: stop on the field-property side and leave a minimal sample.
- The report actually points to the variant name: open a separate record; do not use the field tree as a substitute.
- Only one of the first or second remote derive results is present: record it as unreproduced; do not declare it related to renaming.
- The field names in both minimal inputs account for the change: bring the difference back for review.
- The inputs to the two remote derive runs differ: stop the comparison and unify the inputs first.

## Additional note in the review-page margin

During review, someone reminded us not to write "the rule name can be read at case.rs" as "all derivation paths are determined by this file." This page keeps that entry so that troubleshooting can begin with the naming rules, not to locate the implementation for remote derive.

Another reminder is that if an old fixture has no field properties, it is still possible to look at the variant rule first as a quick screening step; however, the screening result cannot become a conclusion about property precedence. As soon as an explicit field name appears in the incident, or enum and variant both have rules, the investigation must return to the three-layer record.

## Retained old method

> Old method: first apply a variant rule to the structural variant, then look at the field result.
>
> This can still be used as the observation order in temporary samples without explicit field names, but it is no longer used to determine precedence.

remote derive still lacks a record that can be run twice consecutively. The next time it occurs, first place the content or diagnostics from the two runs side by side, then decide whether a separate path needs to be opened.
